content_voiceover: This slide maps hemoglobin destruction, comparing extravascular and intravascular hemolysis — high yield for boards. In extravascular hemolysis, splenic macrophages phagocytose red cells, breaking heme into iron, protoporphyrin, and unconjugated bilirubin, which is conjugated in the liver and excreted as urobilinogen. In intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobin is released directly into plasma, first bound by haptoglobin — which is why haptoglobin falls with intravascular hemolysis. Once haptoglobin is saturated, free hemoglobin is filtered by the kidney, reabsorbed as hemosiderin, or excreted as hemoglobinuria, while excess heme binds hemopexin and albumin as methemalbumin. Across both mechanisms, shared findings of hemolysis include anemia, elevated reticulocytes from marrow compensation, elevated LDH, and elevated indirect bilirubin. The distinguishing feature of intravascular hemolysis is hemoglobinemia and hemoglobinuria, while spherocytes on the smear point toward extravascular, often immune-mediated destruction.
keypoints: Extravascular: splenic macrophages → unconj. bilirubin, urobilinogen
Intravascular: free Hb binds haptoglobin (↓Hp) → filtered by kidney
keypoint_voiceover: Know the shared markers of hemolysis — anemia, elevated reticulocytes, elevated LDH, and elevated indirect bilirubin. What separates the two mechanisms is intravascular hemolysis causing hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, and a drop in haptoglobin, since haptoglobin gets consumed clearing free hemoglobin. Extravascular hemolysis instead shows spherocytes on smear, from splenic macrophages nibbling away red cell membrane.
